articles.title: Ensemble-based uncertainty enables large-scale 3D segmentation quality control in population imaging.
articles.abstract: Modern Deep-Learning facilitates automatic segmentation in large imaging studies. To prevent segmentation errors from impacting data analysis, automated quality control (QC) for filtering segmentations and identifying errors (segmentation selection) is essential. QC must be fast and require minimal expert delineations for application to various ROIs in large datasets. Uncertainty quantification methods capable of estimating segmentation error without ground truth offer a promising foundation. However, their implicit error estimation may lack accuracy, making suitability for segmentation selection unclear. Unfortunately, commonly employed evaluation measures cannot capture their segmentation selection capability. Furthermore, selecting or rejecting segmentations based on uncertainty alone can be non-trivial. We propose a new method for efficient segmentation QC in large imaging cohorts. We comprehensively evaluate uncertainty-based error estimators with respect to key goals of large-scale QC, specifically assessing segmentation selection capability through the area under the risk-coverage-curve. To optimize selection and rejection, we employ a binary search for decision thresholds, balancing the risk of including errors and unnecessarily rejecting segmentations. In >11 000 MRI liver and lung segmentations in the German National Cohort, error estimation using the pairwise Dice of ensemble outputs achieved excellent QC, including segmentation selection. Numerous manually hard-to-detect errors and abnormalities (n>400) were identified during high-quality result selection, measurably restoring integrity of volume and fat measurements. QC was fast (0.29-4.48s/case) and required minimal annotated image data (n<125). Our method can help tackle the challenge of reliable automated QC in large-scale segmentation studies.

articles.title: Meta-PET: A graininess-modulated test-time adaptive network for low-count PET denoising.
articles.abstract: Fast low-count PET imaging shortens acquisition time, enhances patient comfort, and improves clinical workflow efficiency. These benefits have attracted increasing attention in both clinical practice and research. However, reducing the count level to accelerate acquisition degrades image quality, motivating extensive studies on improving low-count PET denoising. Most existing methods are developed for a single count level and lack the flexibility to handle multiple or arbitrary count conditions within one unified model. Joint multi-count training can leverage richer information across different count levels but often leads to domain shifts and performance compromises. Although condition-aware strategies improve generalization by incorporating noise-level information during training, their inference process typically remains parameter-fixed, limiting their ability to adapt explicitly to the noise statistics of each individual unseen input. Toward this challenge, we propose Meta-PET, an adaptive PET denoising framework that combines the strengths of multi-count learning and test-time adaptation. Inspired by model-agnostic meta-learning, Meta-PET is trained to acquire parameters that can be rapidly adapted to new noise conditions through limited self-supervised updates. Rather than beginning from random weights, the model utilizes a joint-learned prior obtained from multi-count training, providing a more structured and generalizable starting point for meta-training scheme. During inference, Meta-PET performs inner-loop self-supervised optimization to align its parameters with the noise statistics of each individual input, enabling flexible and data-specific adaptation without retraining. Moreover, the proposed graininess-aware module directs the model toward noise-sensitive regions while constraining adaptation to fewer tunable parameters, making Meta-PET more efficient and stable during adaptation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that Meta-PET achieves quantitative accuracy and visual fidelity comparable to individually trained single-count models, while maintaining superior consistency across multiple count levels and representative existing methods.

articles.title: Ask Before You Look: A conversational multi-level pathology segmentation framework.
articles.abstract: The development of AI co-pilots for digital pathology requires models that can understand clinical queries expressed in natural language and produce reliable segmentation masks. However, existing benchmarks generally assume that the queried target is present, leaving target-absent cases largely underexplored. Consequently, current language-guided segmentation models are not explicitly trained to determine whether a queried target exists and may hallucinate non-empty masks when it is absent. To address this limitation, we propose COMPASS, a COnversational Multi-level PAthology Segmentation System, which unifies target-presence verification and segmentation in a single end-to-end framework through an "Ask Before You Look" strategy. Target-presence verification is formulated as a supervised visual question answering objective and jointly optimized with the segmentation objective, allowing verification supervision to shape the shared representations used for segmentation. Beyond target verification, accurate pathology segmentation requires both fine-grained morphological information and broader tissue context. We therefore adopt pathology-oriented sparse multi-level feature fusion, where CKA-Spectral Anchor Selection selects complementary SAM-H encoder layers based on pathology-domain representational similarity. We further construct TumorVQA+, an explanation-augmented target-presence verification dataset, and ReasonPath, a pathologist-reviewed reasoning segmentation dataset. Experiments on tissue- and cell-level pathology benchmarks show that COMPASS improves language-guided pathology segmentation, reduces target-absent hallucination, and generates natural language explanations for segmented tumor regions.

articles.title: Estimating performance for safe deployment of machine learning models.
articles.abstract: The main challenge in applying deep neural networks to real-world scenarios lies in distributional discrepancies between training and test datasets, often caused by variations in data acquisition conditions. Assessing the performance of pre-trained models without labels is crucial for safety, but this is complicated by deep models' overly optimistic probabilistic outputs, often exacerbated by class imbalances, leading to unreliable predictions. To address these issues, we introduce MOVAL, a novel MOdel eVALuation tool that estimates performance using unlabeled test data. MOVAL incorporates class-wise confidence calibration to adjust model outputs, allowing for the estimation of metrics beyond accuracy and mitigating the detrimental effects of class imbalance on confidence calibration. Additionally, we propose an ensemble approach that combines multiple calibrated confidence scores for a more robust solution. We validate MOVAL on natural and medical image datasets with various acquisition shifts, covering tasks from classification to segmentation. It achieves state-of-the-art results across evaluation metrics such as accuracy, F1-Score, AUC, and more. Furthermore, we demonstrate that MOVAL provides accurate performance estimations at the class, instance, and pixel levels, ensuring the transparent and safe deployment of machine learning models. We provide MOVAL as a deployment tool for monitoring and estimating performance under a range of domain shifts.

articles.title: Decoding tumor heterogeneity using MRI for predicting response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in hepatocellular carcinoma: a multicenter study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Tumor heterogeneity hinders accurate prediction of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We developed a habitat model using routine in-phase (IP) and opposed-phase (OP) MRI sequences, which provide complementary structure- and lipid-related information, to predict response to ICI therapy in HCC. METHODS: This study included 883 HCC patients from six institutions and public databases. We developed habitat, radiomics, peritumoral, clinical, and combined models to predict partial response (PR) in five institutions. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to evaluate survival differences based on prediction scores. Habitat model interpretability was assessed using Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) along with multi-omics and pathological analyses in the public databases and one external institution. RESULTS: The habitat model showed numerically higher AUCs among the independent models, with AUCs of 0.923, 0.918, and 0.897 in the training set and two external validation sets, respectively. The combined model also showed favorable performance with AUCs of 0.959, 0.965, and 0.955, respectively. Calibration curves showed generally close agreement, while decision curve analyses suggested potential clinical net benefit of the habitat and combined models. Patients with higher habitat scores had significantly longer progression‑free and overall survival (all P < 0.05). Exploratory biological analyses showed that the higher habitat score group was associated with enhanced immune activity, downregulated fatty acid-related pathways, and shorter tumor-inflammatory spatial distances. CONCLUSION: The IP and OP MRI-based habitat model showed potential for treatment-response prediction and prognostic stratification in patients with HCC receiving ICI therapy.

articles.title: CT attenuation changes across freeze-thaw preservation states in donated bodies: a preliminary multi-organ anatomical analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To establish the thermal preservation state as a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT of donated bodies, with the aim of enabling reliable multi-donor comparisons, improving the performance of automated segmentation tools, and providing a translational experimental model applicable to CT-guided thermal interventions. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Eight body donors underwent whole-body CT in up to three preservation states: fresh, frozen (- 20 °C), and thawed. CT datasets were automatically segmented using TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer. Mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values were extracted for major organs and tissue groups. The primary analysis was within-donor: Friedman tests with Wilcoxon signed-rank post-hoc comparisons in donors with complete data (n = 7), complemented by linear mixed-effects models using all available scans. RESULTS: Freezing produced a consistent reduction in CT attenuation across all soft tissues and muscle, with near-complete recovery after thawing. In the primary repeated-measures analysis, preservation state had a significant effect after FDR correction in six of the nine tissue groups (liver, spleen, brain, aorta, pancreas and muscle; q = 0.023-0.042), but not in kidney, heart or bone. Brain and pancreas showed the strongest effects (Kendall's W = 0.80 and 0.76). In the liver, the median within-donor change was - 59.7 HU at freezing and + 60.3 HU at thawing. Mixed-effects models confirmed a significant reduction at freezing in liver, spleen, brain, kidney, pancreas and muscle (β = -35.1 to -52.7 HU) and no residual difference after thawing in any tissue group. Bone attenuation remained stable across all preservation states. CONCLUSION: Freeze-thaw preservation systematically alters CT attenuation in soft tissues while minimally affecting bone. Preservation state should therefore be considered a critical pre-analytical variable in quantitative post-mortem CT, particularly for studies relying on automated segmentation, radiomics, and translational applications involving thermal tissue imaging.

The mismatch between PRISMA and AMSTAR-2: Does adherence to one standard set authors up to fail another?
articles.abstract: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement and AMSTAR-2 are widely used to support the reporting and methodological appraisal of systematic reviews, respectively. Although conceptually complementary, the frameworks are not fully aligned. Consequently, reviews that adhere closely to PRISMA 2020 may receive low AMSTAR-2 confidence ratings. Five recent PRISMA-compliant meta-analyses published in European Radiology illustrate this disconnect: all were rated as having "low" AMSTAR-2 confidence as they failed to provide a detailed list and justification of excluded studies and to report the funding sources of included studies, requirements emphasised by AMSTAR-2 but not formulated as equivalent standalone requirements in PRISMA 2020. Similar patterns have been reported in other clinical fields, suggesting structural misalignment rather than uniformly poor methodological quality. The discrepancy is amplified by AMSTAR-2's designation of critical domains, whereby a single unmet critical item can substantially lower the overall confidence rating, as well as by ambiguity in interpreting certain criteria. Although AMSTAR-2 was intended to support contextual methodological appraisal rather than simple scoring, it is frequently applied as a rigid checklist. Better alignment could include more graduated AMSTAR-2 judgements, clearer appraisal guidance, and incorporation into PRISMA of selected methodological elements emphasised by AMSTAR-2. Ultimately, journals, reviewers, and authors should distinguish reporting completeness from methodological quality and apply both frameworks thoughtfully, transparently, and with appropriate contextual judgement. KEY POINTS: Question Why can PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic reviews receive low AMSTAR-2 confidence ratings? Findings There is structural misalignment between AMSTAR-2 and PRISMA 2020 requirements, and failure to meet a single critical item in AMSTAR-2 can substantially lower the overall rating. Clinical relevance Better alignment between the frameworks and more context-sensitive appraisal are needed to avoid misleading assessments of systematic reviews.

Per-Channel Complex  B 1 +   Mapping for Parallel Transmit Ultra-High Field MRI.
articles.abstract: Ultra-high field (UHF, B0 ≥ 7 T) MRI provides substantial gains in signal-to-noise ratio, spatial resolution and contrast. Routine clinical deployment has been limited by challenges of transmit field (  B 1 +   ) inhomogeneity and specific absorption rate (SAR). Parallel transmission (pTx) can mitigate these challenges but it requires per-channel complex  B 1 +   maps to design effective pTx pulses. We review established and emerging approaches to obtain these maps. We begin by summarising the underlying physical principles and theory. Then we describe methods for magnitude  B 1 +   mapping such as actual flip-angle imaging (AFI), saturation-prepared  B 1 +   mapping (e.g., satTFL) and dual refocusing echo acquisition mode (DREAM) that are the basis of widely-applied per-channel complex  B 1 +   mapping methods, as well as methods of pedagogical and/or historical relevance. Next, we describe how relative  B 1 +   mapping with low-flip angle gradient-recalled echo (GRE) scans can determine the relative phases (and relative magnitudes) of  B 1 +   for each channel. We recap the important interferometric approach that is now widely used. We explain how magnitude and phase maps are combined into complex per-channel  B 1 +   maps. We discuss remaining arbitrary factors such as the position-dependent transmit reference phase. We discuss recent practical implementations such as Sandwich TFL, 3DREAM, compressed-sensing SA2RAGE and respiratory-resolved  B 1 +   mapping. We explore the workflow improvements that could accrue if per-channel  B 1 +   maps do not need to be acquired for every subject. This includes deep-learning-based approaches to synthesize  B 1 +   maps from the normal localiser scans, the universal pulses (UPs) approach to precalibrate pulses and variants such as standardised universal pulses (SUPs), Fast-Online Customised (FOCUS) and machine-learning online customisation. We hope to encourage greater openness and harmonisation of these critical calibration steps for parallel transmit pulse design. This will become increasingly important as 7-T pTx MRI is adopted for multisite cross-vendor clinical research studies and to deliver the full scientific potential of new extremely high field human MRIs.

Can reduced tube voltage CT imaging obviate the need for the arterial phase in patients with undifferentiated acute abdominal pain?
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic performance in abdominal low-kV (kilo-voltage) contrast-enhanced CT (CE-CT) of patients from the emergency department (ED) between venous-phase-only reading sessions and arterial-venous-phase reading sessions. METHODS: 96 patients (mean age 54 years, +/- 17, 49 men) who presented at the ED with undifferentiated abdominal pain underwent multiphasic low-kV CT including at least late arterial phase (LAP) and portal venous phase (PVP). Two reviewers, (Reader 1-board certified radiologist with subspecialization in gastrointestinal imaging and Reader 2-advanced resident with experience in gastrointestinal imaging), analyzed the PVP and LAP independently and determined the most appropriate diagnosis. LAP and PVP images were compared to a reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of the PVP for both readers were calculated. Incremental diagnostic value of the LAP was evaluated. RESULTS: The PVP showed sensitivity, specificity and accuracy in detecting relevant pathology of 93.2%, 87.5% and 92.7% in Reader 1 and 89.8%, 75.0% and 88.5% in Reader 2, respectively with concordant results in 85.4%. There were no findings exclusively detectable in the LAP relevant for clinical management, however it caused approximately 40% of the radiation dose. CONCLUSION: PVP-only imaging with low-kV technique reduced radiation exposure while providing sufficient diagnostic information, suggesting selective use of additional arterial phase for a specific patient group with suspicious vascular emergencies.

articles.title: Monte Carlo simulation of a neuroimaging acquisition with MAPSSIC, a β+sensitive intracerebral microprobe for awake and freely moving rats.
articles.abstract: Establishing robust correlations between molecular neuroimaging and behavioral studies is essential in preclinical research to advance our understanding of brain function and to critically assess the translational relevance of animal models in drug development.Achieving this goal, however, requires imaging animals while they are awake and freely moving -an ongoing challenge, as most preclinical imaging techniques rely on anesthesia.Approach: To overcome the limitations imposed by anesthesia, the MAPSSIC project aims to develop a novel implantable pixelated probe based on Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), designed for use in awake, freely moving rats. By virtue of its direct implantation within the targeted brain regions, the MAPSSIC probe enables the local detection of short-range β+particles emitted by radiotracers, in contrast to conventional micro-PET systems that rely on detecting coincident annihilation γ-rays. In this study, we present Monte Carlo simulations of a typical in vivo brain imaging experiment using [11C]Raclopride, a commonly employed β+-emitting radiotracer, to evaluate the probe's performance.Main results: Results show that over 93 % of detected events originate from particles emitted within the first 2 mm surrounding the probe while also allowing to quantify variations of 5 % to 30 % of the non-displaceable binding potential (BPND) with discrepancy of less than 4 % compared to micro-PET.Significance: This Monte Carlo study demonstrates the device's ability to capture small variations of BPNDbased on spatially localized information, validating its suitability for quantitative kinetic analysis in brain structures such as the striatum.

articles.title: 3D ultrasound shear wave elastography quantifies myocardial stiffness and anisotropy in the human heart.
articles.abstract: Myocardial stiffness (MS) is a key property of diastolic cardiac function which is altered in various cardiomyopathies. Its quantitative evaluation remains challenging due to the myocardium's complex anisotropic fiber architecture and dynamic contraction. We developed a novel 3D shear wave elastography (3D-SWE) system suitable for clinical translation based on 3D ultrafast volumetric imaging for the quantitative assessment of myocardial stiffness in the human heart. Validation was performed on calibrated phantoms and ex vivo in porcine hearts compared to standard 2D-SWE. In vivo feasibility was demonstrated on healthy volunteers and patients with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. We demonstrated that 3D shear wave propagation can be observed in vivo and that 3D-SWE provides quantitative assessment of myocardium anisotropy through shear wave velocities along and across fibers and fractional anisotropy. In addition, myocardial stiffness was significantly elevated in cardiac amyloidosis patients compared to normal myocardium, whereas the fractional anisotropy was decreased. The feasibility of volumetric myocardial stiffness mapping on the human heart was demonstrated showing the potential of 3D-SWE as a clinically oriented tool for early diagnosis of cardiomyopathies such as cardiac amyloidosis.

articles.title: 3D non-rigid motion correction using doppler-regularized optical flow for coronary ultrasound localization microscopy in beating heart.
articles.abstract: Coronary microvascular disease, involving vessels smaller than 300 µm, contributes significantly to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. However, direct visualization of coronary microcirculation remains challenging because current clinical imaging modalities lack the spatial and temporal resolution required to resolve the microvascular network. Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) enables imaging beyond the diffraction limit and can reveal coronary microvascular structures but is altered by large motion. This work addresses 3D non-rigid motion in coronary ULM to enable more accurate reconstruction and visualization of the coronary microvascular network.Approach: Here we developed a 3D non-rigid motion correction framework based on Optical Flow with Doppler velocity regularization to compensate for cardiac motion in 3D ULM of beating rat hearts. Main results: The method was validated in perfused ex vivo beating rat hearts imaged with ultrafast 3D ultrasound. Motion correction enhanced microbubbles tracking density and vessels delineation, enabling visualization of microvessels below 100 µm and velocity measurements with spatial resolution of at least 40 µm. Significance: This framework advances volumetric assessment of coronary microcirculation, facilitating longer acquisition windows and may support future cardiovascular research and clinical applications by overcoming motion-induced limitations in 3D coronary ULM.

articles.title: Lessons in IR: Permanent Paraplegia Following Chemical Neurolysis of Splanchnic Nerves.
Diagnostic performance benchmarks of MRI for prostate cancer: a large-scale cohort study of 33,759 patients.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the real-world diagnostic performance of PI-RADS for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) across large-scale worldwide cohorts. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This multicenter observational study included 20,429 patients from nine Chinese institutions and a published worldwide meta-analysis dataset comprising 13,330 patients for comparison. All PI-RADS assessments were extracted from original MRI reports produced by clinical radiologists as part of standard diagnostic workflows. Summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed using a bivariate random-effects model, and center-level areas under the curve (AUCs) were pooled via random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted. RESULTS: PI-RADS exhibited overall discriminatory performance for csPCa across nine Chinese cohorts comparable to the META results from 70 studies, though significant inter-center variation was observed. Using a PI-RADS ≥ 3 threshold, pooled sensitivity was 92.6% and specificity was 51.5%. At a PI-RADS ≥ 4 threshold, pooled specificity improved to 78.1%, with a sensitivity of 81.5%. The overall diagnostic performance was consistent across thresholds: The summary ROC (SROC) AUC was 0.903 for PI-RADS ≥ 3 and 0.826 for PI-RADS ≥ 4 in detecting csPCa at the meta-analysis level. Subgroup analyses indicated better performance among older patients (≥ 70 years) and those with higher PSA levels (> 20 ng/mL). PI-RADS v2.1 outperformed v2 or earlier versions in most clinical scenarios. CONCLUSIONS: This large-scale real-world study provides critical multicenter evidence supporting the use of PI-RADS in clinical practice worldwide, while also revealing substantial variability in scoring and diagnostic performance across institutions. The findings offer an evidence-based overview of PI-RADS implementation in China and worldwide, highlighting both its utility and inconsistencies. KEY POINTS: Question What are the real-world PI-RADS diagnostic performance benchmarks for clinically significant prostate cancer detection across diverse Chinese multicenter institutions versus global data? Findings PI-RADS demonstrated good overall performance (SROC AUC 0.903 at a threshold of ≥ 3), with superior discriminatory ability in older patients, higher PSA levels, and v2.1 users. Critical relevance statement This article critically assesses substantial inter-institutional heterogeneity in PI-RADS performance, highlighting that pooled estimates should not replace local calibration and that regionally adapted implementation strategies are essential for advancing clinical radiology practice.

articles.title: Pediatric portal venous dimensions: a computed tomography-based normative study utilizing multiplanar reformation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Paediatric portal vein reference values are derived almost exclusively from ultrasound, which systematically yields smaller measurements than CT. CT-specific normative data for children are limited to a single study that did not include multiplanar reformation (MPR) measurements, splenic vein data, or comprehensive anthropometric analysis. OBJECTIVE: To establish CT-based reference values for the portal venous system in children and adolescents, including both axial and MPR measurements of the main portal vein, and to characterize the systematic discrepancy between the two measurement methods. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this single-centre retrospective study, 1,101 children aged 0-17 years who underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT between January 2018 and April 2026 were included after applying strict exclusion criteria. Main portal vein (axial and MPR), right portal vein, left portal vein, and splenic vein diameters were measured independently by two radiologists. Age- and body surface area-stratified reference values were generated using locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOESS). RESULTS: MPR measurements exceeded axial measurements in all 1,101 subjects (mean difference 1.2±0.9 mm; proportional bias r=0.523, P<0.001). Age showed the strongest correlation with main portal vein diameter (ρ=0.894). Sex-based differences emerged exclusively in subjects aged ≥13 years (all P≤0.006). The splenic-to-main portal vein ratio remained relatively stable across the paediatric age spectrum (coefficient of variation 8.2%). Interobserver agreement was excellent for all parameters (ICC, 0.986-0.993). CONCLUSION: CT-based portal venous reference values in children differ substantially from ultrasound-derived reference values. MPR measurements systematically exceed axial measurements, particularly in adolescents. Because MPR permits measurement perpendicular to the vessel long axis, use MPR-specific reference values when MPR-based measurements are employed.

articles.title: Feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT for resectable HCC evaluation: lesion detection and histopathological correlations.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the feasibility of one-stop multi-energy dynamic volume perfusion photon-counting CT (VP-PCCT) for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) evaluation, including lesion detection and correlations with histopathology. MATERIALS AND METHODS: From July 2024 to June 2025, 407 participants with suspected malignant liver lesions prospectively underwent VP-PCCT, and 177 patients with pathology-confirmed HCC who received three-phase energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) were retrospectively enrolled for comparisons of image quality and lesion detectability. Single-phase images reconstructed from VP-PCCT perfusion datasets were compared with EID-CT. Perfusion parameters were analyzed between groups stratified separately by histological grade and microvascular invasion (MVI), and logistic regression was employed to identify independent indicators. RESULTS: Ninety-two participants [median age, 62 years (IQR, 53-69); 76 males] with pathology-confirmed HCC were included in the VP-PCCT group and matched with 92 in the EID-CT group. Compared with EID-CT, 40-keV VP-PCCT provided comparable image quality for HCC and vessels with a similar tumor detection rate but a lower radiation dose. Poorly-differentiated HCCs showed higher tumor hepatic perfusion index (HPItumor) and peritumoral blood flow (BFperitumor); MVI-positive HCCs exhibited lower tumor arterial liver perfusion (ALPtumor) and normalized blood flow of peritumoral region (BFnorm_peritumor) (all p < 0.05). HPItumor [odds ratio (OR): 1.06] and BFperitumor (OR: 1.04) were independent risk factors for poorly differentiated HCC, whereas decreased ALPtumor (OR: 0.97) and BFnorm_peritumor (OR: 0.25) were associated with MVI positivity (all p < 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: One-stop VP-PCCT delivers high-quality morphologic and perfusion evaluation in a single low-dose scan, with hemodynamic profiles that may be associated with histological grade and MVI status. KEY POINTS: Question Clinical use of dynamic volume perfusion CT for comprehensively evaluating HCC without additional multiphase contrast-enhanced imaging remains limited. Findings Multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT provided high-quality morphologic imaging of HCC at a low dose, with perfusion parameters independently indicating poorly differentiated HCC and MVI. Critical relevance statement One-stop multi-energy dynamic photon-counting perfusion CT enables high-quality morphologic and functional assessment in a single low-dose scan, providing comprehensive HCC evaluation with hemodynamic profiling that may support the assessment of histological grade and MVI.

articles.title: Middle meningeal artery embolization in chronic subdural hematoma: A real-world multicenter italian experience.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate technical feasibility, short-term radiological outcomes, subsequent surgical intervention, and complications of middle meningeal artery (MMA) embolization for chronic subdural hematoma (CSDH), distinguishing primary embolization from embolization after surgery. METHODS: This retrospective study included 228 consecutive patients undergoing attempted MMA embolization at three Italian referral centers between January 2019 and November 2024. Technical success was the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included radiological success, defined as residual hematoma thickness ≤ 6 mm on CT at 60-90 days, subsequent surgical evacuation, and procedure-related complications. Subgroup comparisons were exploratory and used available-case data. RESULTS: Primary embolization was performed in 115 patients and embolization after surgery in 113. Technical success was achieved in 223/228 patients (97.8%). Follow-up CT was available in 188/228 patients (82.5%). Median residual hematoma thickness was 4 mm (interquartile range, 0-8), without a significant difference between groups (p = 0.372). Radiological success occurred in 132/188 patients (70.2%): 57/88 (64.8%) after primary embolization and 75/100 (75.0%) after surgery (p = 0.151). Complications occurred in 7/228 patients (3.1%), including one major ischemic stroke, without a significant between-group difference (p = 0.720). Subsequent surgical evacuation was required in 7/188 patients (3.7%): 5/88 (5.7%) versus 2/100 (2.0%), respectively (p = 0.255). CONCLUSION: MMA embolization demonstrated high technical success, favorable short-term radiological outcomes, and a low rate of subsequent surgical intervention. These findings support its feasibility and potential clinical value in selected patients with CSDH, both as primary treatment and after surgical evacuation. Prospective comparative studies are needed to confirm these observations.

articles.title: Feasibility of Singular Value Decomposition Implementation for 129Xe Hyperpolarized Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (HyperCEST) Molecular Imaging.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a method for enhanced quantification of hyperpolarized chemical exchange saturation transfer (HyperCEST) using singular value decomposition (SVD) for both spectroscopy and molecular imaging. METHODS: Dynamic HyperCEST spectra acquired with cucurbit[6]uril (CB[6]) and resorcinarene trimer methanesulfonate (R3-Noria-MeSO3H) in aqueous solution were subjected to SVD to denoise the magnetic resonance spectra. The HyperCEST depletion spectra were recalculated from SVD-reconstructed data using a standard approach. The on- and off-resonance coronal 129Xe images acquired from R3-Noria-MeSO3H samples in vitro and from three healthy rats post CB[6] injection were also reconstructed using SVD prior to pixel-by-pixel HyperCEST map calculation. A localized variance of the HyperCEST values was calculated. RESULTS: A paired t-test demonstrated a statistically significant increase (up to ∼13%) in localized HyperCEST values both in vivo (in the animal kidneys and aorta) and in vitro (across the phantom volume) due to the SVD incorporation. In addition, SVD significantly reduced HyperCEST variance. The HyperCEST variance for in vivo images was reduced by 32.3%, whereas the variance for in vitro images was reduced by 36%. The SNR of the SVD-reconstructed images and spectra was significantly higher. The SVD resulted in a significant improvement of the shape of HyperCEST depletion spectra and maximized the HyperCEST effect in the case of CB[6] for lower depolarization angles. CONCLUSION: Implementation of the proposed SVD-based method is beneficial for 129Xe HyperCEST molecular imaging due to significantly improved quantification of the HyperCEST effect, reduced variability of the localized HyperCEST values, and significantly improved quality of the HyperCEST depletion spectra.

articles.title: Deep-Reorder: Refined Motion Correction for 3D Brain MRI via Iterative Data Regrouping.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Accurate and temporally high-resolution estimation of subject motion is paramount for effective motion-correction in MRI. This work proposes a novel approach for estimating subject motion within a 3D MRI scan with high temporal resolution. METHODS: Starting from an incoherent sampling scheme, images are reconstructed from temporally ordered k-space fractions via deep learning, enabling motion estimation via registration between each image. Assuming the bulk of the motion is removed using these initial estimates, the remaining misalignment between k-space fractions is expected to be minimally correlated in time. Based on this insight, an iterative strategy is proposed in which shots are arbitrarily regrouped into new k-space fractions, regardless of their original temporal ordering, for subsequent motion estimation and correction. This effectively increases the temporal resolution of the approach, enabling individual correction of all shots. RESULTS: When applied to 3D T1w TFE MRI of the brain, the proposed approach "Deep-Reorder" estimated a unique motion state for all shots, producing significantly better estimations of retrospective motion compared to estimation without iterative data regrouping. On prospectively motion-corrupted scans with intentional head movement by volunteers, the proposed approach consistently improved image quality, producing less noisy images with reduced motion artifacts. CONCLUSION: In conclusion, the proposed approach, which is free of external tracking devices or navigators, effectively estimated 3D motion and corrected motion artifacts with increased temporal resolution.

articles.title: An anatomy-aware spatio-temporal generative extrapolation network for distal ascending aorta restoration in standard echocardiographic views.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), the standard parasternal long-axis (PLAX) view enables reliable evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root. Owing to the limited field of view of the ultrasound probe and rib-window occlusion, the distal ascending aorta (AA) is frequently truncated, compromising the diagnosis of aortic aneurysm and dilation. PURPOSE: We aim to address the incomplete visualization of the distal AA in standard PLAX views. By aggregating fragmented anatomical features intermittently visible in adjacent frames, we enhance the clarity of vessel wall edges and generate the distal AA structure, thereby completing the missing AA imagery in standard PLAX views. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively collected 1160 TTE videos from Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (August 2022 - December 2024), all showing complete AA anatomy. After de-identification, 1059 cases were randomly split into training/validation/test sets (6:2:2), and 101 cases were reserved for observer agreement experiments. An additional 152 videos from three different device models (EPIQ CVX, GE Voluson E10, Resona A20T) formed an external validation set. Two training data types were constructed: (i) dual-view synchronous data - a standard PLAX sequence and an AO-PLAX sequence acquired after a cranial probe shift, phase-matched at end diastole (ED); and (ii) locally masked data - the distal AA region was masked, forcing the model to infer missing anatomy from left-side context. Input sequences of five frames (ED ± 2) were extracted. The proposed Spatio-Temporal Ascending-Aorta generative adversarial network (STAA-GAN) first aligns adjacent frames using an Edge Boosted Feature Alignment (EBFA) module with multi-stage modulated deformable convolutions. A channel-wise fusion strategy then aggregates temporally aligned features. The fused representation is fed into a Swin-UNet generator enhanced with a Strip based Cross window Prediction (SCP) module to capture long-range structural dependencies. Training employs a composite loss including pixel reconstruction, feature reconstruction, texture consistency, relativistic average least-squares GAN (RaLSGAN), temporal coherence, and structure-aware terms, with data-dependent weighting. Statistical analyzes included Bland-Altman, Passing-Bablok regression, paired t-tests with Cohen's d, Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and two one-sided tests (TOST, Δ = 0.2  cm  ). RESULTS: STAA-GAN achieved the best image-quality values among the compared methods, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) = 22.51 dB, structural similarity index (SSIM) = 0.7574, multi-scale structural similarity index (MS-SSIM) = 0.8598, and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) = 0.1758. All 12 pairwise comparisons (SRN, IOH, and U-Transformer versus STAA-GAN, designated as the reference group) remained statistically significant after Bonferroni correction (  α 1 = 0.00417  ), with absolute effect sizes ranging from 0.255 to 3.439. The per-frame inference time was 203 ms. In clinical consistency validation, the mean difference between measurements on generated and original images was ≤ 0.01   cm with 95% limits of agreement within ± 0.13   cm; TOST with Δ = 0.2   cm confirmed clinical equivalence for all comparisons ( p < 0.001  ). The segmentation Dice coefficient on generated images averaged 0.913 ± 0.045  across five cross-validation folds. External validation on three different ultrasound devices (Philips, GE, Mindray) maintained consistent equivalence (TOST p < 0.001  , Cohen's d < 0.2  ). These results demonstrate that STAA-GAN produces clinically interchangeable distal ascending aorta images with high fidelity and real-time feasibility. CONCLUSIONS: STAA-GAN enables extrapolation of the missing distal ascending aorta in standard PLAX views, achieving improved image quality and clinically equivalent diameter measurements on both internal and external validation datasets. These findings support its potential for assisting distal ascending aorta assessment in routine echocardiography.

articles.title: A public projection imaging dataset for fieldfree line magnetic particle imaging.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is an emerging biomedical imaging modality. In recent years, human-scale MPI systems based on field-free line MPI (FFL-MPI) projection imaging have been increasingly advanced. However, the lack of publicly available FFL-MPI datasets has hindered algorithm development and system performance optimization. To address this issue, this paper presents a dataset based on the FFL-MPI system, named FFL-MPI-Data, through simulation studies and data acquisition from a real-world system. ACQUISITION AND VALIDATION METHODS: The FFL-MPI-Data contains both simulated and measured data spanning multiple domains and harmonics. The measured dataset was acquired using a self-developed scanner, which collected raw voltage signals, sinograms, and reconstructed images from 100 physical phantoms. The simulated dataset was generated via a custom-built simulation framework that replicates the key parameters of the experimental scanner, with the MNIST dataset employed as digital phantoms. The simulation framework is validated by evaluating the characteristics of harmonic images output from numerical phantoms. Furthermore, the utility and reliability of the dataset were verified by evaluating the performance of a deep learning model (FBPConvNet) on both sparse-angle and limited-angle reconstruction tasks. DATA FORMAT AND USAGE NOTES: The FFL-MPI-Data repository adopts the Hierarchical Data Format (HDF5) for data storage, which contains both phantom data and associated metadata. The dataset is publicly available on the Zenodo platform. Furthermore, we provide open-source codes for data processing, image reconstruction, simulation implementation, and deep learning demonstrations at https://github.com/BUAALGH/FFL-MPI-Data. Users can readily access and utilize the FFL-MPI-Data dataset via the provided example code. POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS: FFL-MPI-Data represents a publicly accessible dataset for FFL-MPI, addressing the scarcity of available data for projection imaging research in this domain. This dataset is expected to facilitate the development and validation of image reconstruction algorithms, including investigations into signal processing, multi-domain reconstruction, and multi-harmonic reconstruction for specific tasks such as sparse-angle and limited-angle reconstruction.

articles.title: Robustness of proliferation-based constrained spatiotemporal fractionation under setup and radiobiological uncertainties in liver radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Spatiotemporal fractionation redistributes dose between fractions and may reduce normal-tissue exposure. Its sensitivity to setup uncertainty and radiobiological assumptions requires evaluation before clinical use. PURPOSE: To evaluate proliferation-based constrained spatiotemporal fractionation (p-cSTF) under geometric and radiobiological perturbations in conventionally fractionated liver radiotherapy. The focus was normal-liver dose. METHODS: Thirty-five patients with hepatocellular carcinoma were included. Uniform fractionation, proliferation-based spatiotemporal fractionation (p-STF), and p-cSTF were evaluated over 25 fractions. The primary comparison matched nominal mean gross tumor volume (GTV) biologically effective dose (BED); a supplementary comparison matched nominal model-derived tumor control probability (TCP). Setup tests comprised 18 single-axis offsets (± 1, ± 2, and ± 3 mm) and 24 transverse voxel offsets, each held constant over treatment. Thirty scenarios varied biological-model parameters; precision checks used two 480-scenario sequences. Nominal dose grids were evaluated under perturbations without reoptimization. Endpoints included physical dose, BED, equivalent dose in 2 Gy fractions (EQD2), coverage, and response-model scores. RESULTS: Under biological-parameter variation, normal-liver (liver excluding GTV) BED was 26.22 ± 7.00 Gy for p-cSTF, 28.18 ± 7.57 Gy for Uniform, and 28.05 ± 7.76 Gy for p-STF. Corresponding EQD2 values were 14.92 ± 3.96, 16.05 ± 4.29, and 15.96 ± 4.39 Gy. Values are cohort means and between-patient standard deviations of patient-specific scenario means. Normal-liver BED remained lower with p-cSTF after nominal TCP matching, although fixed transverse offsets produced lower GTV TCP than with Uniform. Expanded sampling retained the direction of the liver-dose difference; the original 30 scenarios did not meet the specified precision criteria for scenario variability. CONCLUSIONS: P-cSTF retained a simulated normal-liver dose advantage under the tested perturbations, including after nominal TCP matching. This advantage must be considered alongside target-response trade-offs and uncertainty in scenario-variability estimates. Clinical toxicity and treatment deliverability were not evaluated.

articles.title: Diffusion Prior-Driven Vision-Language Adaptation for Few-Shot Medical Anomaly Detection.
articles.abstract: Unsupervised medical anomaly detection faces dual challenges of pathological data scarcity and domain gaps when transferring general-purpose vision-language models to fine-grained tasks. This study aims to address the misalignment between global semantic representations and local pathological nuances by proposing a novel hybrid supervision framework. We propose a flexible vision-language adaptation framework in which diffusion-based pseudo-anomaly synthesis serves as an optional training enhancement. For CheXpert and BUSI, region-guided diffusion generates localized pseudo-anomalies to provide additional discriminative supervision. For BrainMRI, the framework is trained exclusively on normal reference images without any synthetic anomaly augmentation, allowing us to assess its effectiveness independently of the diffusion synthesis component. The architecture incorporates a local-enhanced feature rectifier to enhance local textural representation, a zero-initialized hypersphere-aligned residual adapter for stable cross-modal manifold alignment, and a temperature-scaled mapmaker for multi-scale dense anomaly localization. Performance was evaluated across three medical imaging modalities under multiple few-shot configurations. Our method remains highly competitive compared to state-of-the-art approaches in terms of image-level detection and pixel-level localization. On the ultrasound dataset under a 32-shot setting, the framework achieved an image-level area under the curve of 94.2% and a pixel-level area under the curve of 96.6%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework across the evaluated medical imaging modalities under different training configurations. In particular, its competitive performance on BrainMRI without synthetic anomaly augmentation suggests that the vision-language adaptation framework can remain effective when offline pseudo-anomaly generation is unavailable. The code involved in this study is publicly available on website https://github.com/SWLee777/DiffVLA .

articles.title: Propagation of Low-Dose-Induced Noise Characteristics Across Deep Learning Layers in CT Imaging.
articles.abstract: Dose reduction in computed tomography (CT) imaging impacts diagnostic accuracy for human observers and potentially artificial intelligence (AI) systems. As noise propagates through an AI model, its characteristics change, possibly influencing model performance. This study aims to develop a configurable low-dose CT simulation tool in image-space and analyze noise behavior in deep learning (DL) layers. The noise characteristics were quantified using the noise power spectrum (NPS) within homogeneous phantom regions. NPS area under the curve (intensity) and median frequency (texture) were reported. Low-dose CT images were simulated using a custom program that was calibrated for configurable noise intensity and texture. Noise was generated at texture levels. Pre-trained U-Net features were extracted from reference and simulated low-dose images, enabling NPS-based analysis of noise propagation across deep learning layers. NPS from simulated low-dose CT images matched reference NPS for various intensity and texture values. Feature analysis revealed progressive convergence of noise characteristics across deep learning layers, with batch normalization mitigating amplification observed after convolution and ReLU activation. Differences in noise texture between low-dose simulations converge along the U-Net contracting path. The image-space simulation tool offers a viable alternative for researchers lacking access to raw data, supporting future AI-focused dose optimization studies. However, whether these outcomes translate to segmentation performance remains unclear and warrants further investigation.

articles.title: Data Leakage and Unverified Provenance in Public Brain Tumor MRI Datasets: A Systematic Audit.
articles.abstract: Brain tumor MRI classification studies routinely report accuracies above 99%, yet many public datasets in this domain trace to a few original sources and are often combined or cross-validated without accounting for shared origin. We audited seven brain tumor MRI datasets (34,525 images) for leakage within datasets and overlap between datasets typically treated as independent. Internal leakage was detected with perceptual hashing and rotation-aware structural similarity. Cross-dataset overlap was detected with ResNet-50 embedding similarity, checked against a random-pair baseline, a DenseNet-121 sensitivity analysis, and blinded two-rater review (all 75 sampled above-threshold pairs were true duplicates; 95% CI 95.1-100). A further blinded review just below the threshold found roughly half of the sampled pairs were also duplicates, so reported overlap is a lower bound. True-duplicate leakage between training and evaluation splits occurred in three of four datasets with predefined splits, including a peer-reviewed dataset and one documented as overlap-free. For 14 of 16 dataset pairs, 15.6-99.1% of the smaller dataset's images were automatically matched to the other, including datasets described as collected from named hospitals. In a controlled experiment on the one dataset with patient identifiers, image-level splitting yielded higher accuracy than patient-level splitting (97.10 ± 0.69% vs. 91.82 ± 2.77%; Welch's t-test, p = 0.017), with a 10.1-point drop in meningioma F1. This addresses within-dataset correlation only, so it is a conservative estimate of total inflation. Reported performance warrants cautious interpretation, and tooling for verifying dataset independence is lacking. We propose a checklist for dataset creators and researchers.

articles.title: From a Clinical Mammography Archive to an AI-Ready Imaging Cohort: A Single-Center Implementation and Evidence Audit.
articles.abstract: Clinical imaging archives contain potentially valuable research data, but records retained for patient care do not automatically form an analysis-ready cohort. In this single-center study, we implemented and audited a metadata-driven workflow that separated patient-day indexing, image/report availability, study-defined bilateral four-view structure, quality control state, and pathology linkage. Among 13,203 indexed patient-day groups from January 2015 through December 2020, 5390 were DICOM-bearing, and 3169 of these met the metadata-defined bilateral four-view requirement (58.8%). The same requirement was met by 3168 of 5381 DICOM- and report-matched folders (58.9%), whereas 7813 report-linked groups lacked retained DICOM and were not assessable for image structure. Pathology was examined independently rather than as a nested endpoint; the strict-window diagnostic biopsy analysis identified 229 strict-window high-confidence groups. Thus, archive size, joint image/report availability, structural eligibility, and outcome evidence defined different analytical states. This implementation shows how established imaging-informatics principles can make cohort construction auditable within one institution; transferability requires independent external implementation and evaluation.

articles.title: The Deep Learning-Based Prediction Method for Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis of Thyroid Cancer Based on Multimodal Data.
articles.abstract: Thyroid cancer is a common malignant tumor worldwide, and there is a risk of misdiagnosis or over-treatment for small-sized thyroid cancer. The key to eliminating this risk lies in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis. The traditional manual prediction methods are not ideal, so this paper proposes an intelligent prediction method based on deep learning. This method is based on common clinical examination data, including ultrasound images, ultrasound image text descriptions, and blood test data. A deep convolutional neural network model is proposed using data from these three modalities as inputs. The model integrates multimodal data features through mean cross-attention and extracts fine-grained classification information from the fused feature map through a bilinear CNN network, demonstrating strong feature discrimination ability. Through collecting data and conducting various experiments, the experimental results show that the model proposed in this paper has good performance in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis, is better than the manual prediction, and has broad application prospects. Future research will continue to strive for data collection, increasing the amount of collected data and improving multi-center representativeness, and enhancing the diagnostic and predictive capabilities of the network model through technological improvements.

articles.title: Correlation between the IVIM-MRI based tissue perfusion parameters and blood flow index measured by diffuse correlation spectroscopy.
articles.abstract: Intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique evaluates the microstructure and microvascular blood perfusion of biological tissues. IVIM-derived pseudo-diffusion coefficient (Dfast) quantifies the perfusion-related motion of blood within the tissue microvascular and is related to the mean squared displacement of water molecules in time. Diffuse correlation spectroscopy (DCS) is a noninvasive optical technique to monitor the microvascular blood flow changes. DCS-derived blood flow index (BFIDCS) is proportional to mean squared displacement of the red blood cells in time, thereby enabling comparison to Dfast. To evaluate the correlation between Dfast and BFIDCS, controlled muscle-occlusion tests were performed on five healthy volunteers, with five leg and four forearm datasets. In response to muscle occlusion, the BFIDCS decreased, whereas the mean Dfast increased, leading to no positive correlation between these parameters (rrm: repeated measures correlation, rrm=-0.219,95%CI:-0.724to0.438 in leg occlusion and rrm=-0.567,95%CI:-0.894to0.155, in forearm occlusion). The IVIM data were of adequate quality (median voxelwise signal to noise ratio at b = 0: 25-57), however the voxelwise coefficient of variation CVvoxels of the Dfast (median within-subjects CVvoxels in the leg: 210.3% and in forearm: 160.9%) were imprecise. The disagreement between the IVIM- and DCS-derived parameter responses is therefore specific to the applied protocol, and its cause remains unresolved. Therefore, further studies with larger cohorts and different experimental protocols are required to better characterize the correlation between the IVIM- and DCS-derived parameters under varying perfusion conditions.

articles.title: AdaML: Adaptive meta-learning for generalizable sparse-view CT reconstruction.
articles.abstract: Sparse-view CT reduces radiation exposure but renders image reconstruction severely ill-posed. Although deep learning has substantially improved reconstruction quality, most existing models are trained within specific anatomical domains and often degrade under cross-anatomy distribution shifts. To improve reconstruction generalization under limited target-domain supervision, we investigate a meta-learning framework for sparse-view CT reconstruction. However, directly applying Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) to this task is challenging, because CT reconstruction is a high-dimensional inverse problem in which aggressive inner-loop updates can easily induce meta-overfitting and unstable optimization. To address this issue, we first introduce Stable Meta-Learning (StaML), which constructs anatomy-wise tasks and adopts conservative inner-loop updates to learn a more transferable initialization. Building on this, we further propose Adaptive Meta-Learning (AdaML), which dynamically adjusts per-step learning rates during meta-testing to better balance convergence capability and stability. Extensive experiments across multiple CT datasets and anatomical regions, under different k-shot settings, view numbers, and noise levels, demonstrate that AdaML consistently improves reconstruction quality over representative meta-learning and non-meta-learning baselines with favorable convergence. These results suggest that combining stable meta-initialization with adaptive test-time optimization is a promising direction for cross-anatomy sparse-view CT reconstruction. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Stth-er/AdaML.

articles.title: Ultrasound-guided microwave ablation for biopsy-proven breast fibroadenomas ≤3 cm: clinical, imaging, and safety outcomes at 12-month follow-up.
articles.abstract: AIM: The aim of this study was to evaluate the imaging, clinical, and safety outcomes of ultrasound (US)-guided microwave ablation (MWA) for biopsy-proven breast fibroadenomas ≤3.0 cm. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 27 patients with 27 core-biopsy-proven fibroadenomas ≤3.0 cm treated between January and July 2025. MWA was performed for clinical treatment purposes according to a predefined institutional protocol and was not undertaken as part of a prospective research study. Institutional ethics committee approval was subsequently obtained for retrospective review of the clinical and imaging data. US-guided MWA was performed under local anaesthesia using a 2450-MHz system at 40 W. Clinical and US follow-up was performed at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Changes in tumour volume and maximum diameter were evaluated using repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA). RESULTS: The mean MWA duration was 101.3 ± 26.5 s. All 27 procedures were successfully completed. At 12 months, mean maximum tumour diameter decreased from 20.69 ± 6.96 mm to 5.59 ± 1.53 mm, corresponding to a 73.3% reduction. Mean tumour volume decreased from 2.30 ± 1.87 mL to 0.60 ± 0.28 mL, corresponding to a 73.5% reduction (P < .001). Sixteen of 27 lesions achieved >90% volume reduction without residual vascularity on colour Doppler US. No epidermal burns, haematoma, infection, skin depression, or other major adverse events occurred. All patients were satisfied with the cosmetic outcome at 12 months. CONCLUSION: US-guided MWA provided substantial 12-month reduction in size and volume of biopsy-proven fibroadenomas ≤3 cm with favourable safety and cosmetic outcomes. It may represent a minimally invasive treatment option for appropriately selected symptomatic patients who wish to avoid surgical excision.
